newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN does not expect face-off with West on Burma.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN does not expect face-off with West on Burma.

text.p: The secretary-general of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Tuesday brushed aside fears of a confrontation with Western nations over the planned admittance of Burma to the group in July.
Dato Ajit Singh told a news conference both sides wanted the same thing -- positive developments in Burma -- but differed on the best way to achieve this.
He said that ASEAN would have "very frank, very open and very engaging discussions" with Burma once it was a member.

He also told a news briefing the ASEAN agreement last Saturday to admit Burma, Laos and Cambodia at the group's annual foreign ministers' meeting in Kuala Lumpur in late July was basically technical as the political decision had already been made.

The group currently comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Philippines, Vietnam and Brunei, and the admittance of the other three will fulfil the ASEAN founders' dream of bringing all Southeast Asian nations into the fold on its 30th anniversary.
"The political decision was already taken by the ASEAN informal summit in Jakarta in November last year to bring in the three countries," Singh said.
"So the decision that was taken in Kuala Lumpur was not so much a political decision, but the timing was fixed...it was a technical decision because they met all the technical requirements," he said.

The United States had led the way in pressuring ASEAN to delay admitting Burma over its record on democracy and human rights. ASEAN members, however, say they believe a long-standing policy of constructive engagement would have better results than Western-imposed sanctions.
"As far as Washington and ASEAN are concerned on the question of Myanmar (Burma), we have had an honest difference of opinion," Singh said.
"We do have a difference of opinion, but our objectives are the same. Our objectives are to have peace and stability in the region and to see some positive developments in Myanmar.
"The difference is that Washington wants to achieve these goals through enforcing sanctions. ASEAN doesn't believe in that, we believe in the policy of constructive engagement," he said.

The July ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting is followed by meetings with 10 so-called dialogue partners, who include Australia, the United States, India, Canada, China, South Korea, Japan, New Zealand and Russia.
Singh said however under the present system, foreign ministers from outside the area would not find themselves face-to-face in an individual dialogue session with Burma's foreign minister.
